name: Baking soda deodorant

lead: Baking soda deodorant uses sodium bicarbonate, alone or mixed with other ingredients, to keep underarm odour under control so you come across as clean and approachable. It is one of the oldest patented deodorant ingredients and a common home recipe.

It works on odour rather than sweat. Sodium bicarbonate is mildly alkaline and is said to neutralise odour. Reference sources note little evidence that it absorbs odours in general, and no published trials of it as a deodorant were found.

paras: People buy it in commercial deodorants or mix it into home-made pastes and powders, then apply it to clean, dry underarms as part of a natural-deodorant routine. It is often combined with other ingredients, and the effect is felt immediately on application.

Reference sources list eye irritation as its main hazard. Because it is alkaline, some users report underarm irritation, though no published study of this was found. People with sensitive or broken skin may want to avoid it.

angle.text: Users apply sodium bicarbonate deodorants, store-bought or home-made, to keep underarm odour down and present as clean. The smell stays controlled through the day, which reads as a cleaner, more approachable presence. It is among the oldest patented deodorant ingredients.

lead: Baking soda deodorant refers to deodorants made with sodium bicarbonate, either commercial products or home-made mixtures applied to the underarms. People use it to keep armpit odour down so they smell clean and fresh, and it is popular among those who prefer simple or aluminium-free ingredients. Wikipedia lists sodium bicarbonate among early deodorant ingredients and notes it appears in some dry and wet deodorants, alone or combined with other ingredients [1][2].

Sodium bicarbonate is mildly alkaline in solution, and has long been promoted as an odour absorber, although the Wikipedia article on the compound says there is little evidence that it absorbs odours in general [2]. Patent literature includes a 2004 deodorant towelette system soaked in a solution that includes baking soda [3].
No clinical studies of baking soda deodorants were found.
infobox: Deodorants are regulated as cosmetics; antiperspirants as drugs [1]

paras: Home-made versions mix baking soda with other ingredients, and some commercial natural deodorants include it. Body odour arises from bacterial breakdown of apocrine sweat; deodorants either mask odour or act on bacteria, and do not reduce sweat [1][4]. Wikipedia lists a 2004 patented towelette immersed in a solution of baby powder, baking soda, deodorant and water [3].

Wikipedia describes bacteria on the skin, rather than sweat itself, as the cause of most body odour, with apocrine glands in the armpits secreting compounds that skin flora convert to odorous molecules [4].

Wikipedia traces the first modern commercial deodorant, Mum, to Edna Murphey of Philadelphia in 1888, and lists early formulas with ingredients including zinc oxide, acids, ammonium chloride, sodium bicarbonate and formaldehyde, noting that several early ingredients were messy or irritating and that formaldehyde is now recognised as a carcinogen [1]. The first commercial antiperspirant, Everdry, is listed at 1903, and Jules Montenier's modern aluminium chloride formula was patented in 1941 [1]. The deodorant market grew about 600-fold between 1942 and 1957 and by 1957 an estimated half of men used deodorant [1].

Sodium bicarbonate itself has been known since 1801, when Valentin Rose the Younger is credited with its discovery in Berlin [2]. Baking soda re-entered deodorant discussion with the natural-products trend, which also brought alum crystals and other aluminium-free options [1].

Sodium bicarbonate, known since the 1801 work of Valentin Rose the Younger, is amphoteric, reacts with acids to release carbon dioxide, and gives mildly alkaline solutions.[2] Wikipedia's deodorant article discusses acid-based products as aimed at preserving the skin's slightly acidic acid mantle, and notes alkaline soaps can disrupt it.[1] Proponents of baking soda say it neutralises odour; no study located tested this on skin.

Wikipedia notes that crystal deodorants use potassium or ammonium alum, which inhibits bacterial action, and that a 1999 study found synthetic potassium alum crystals were a weak skin irritant linked to crystal deodorant dermatitis [1]. Other options listed include activated charcoal, milk of magnesia, and pH-neutral or acidifying products [1].

The same article states the National Cancer Institute says no scientific evidence links antiperspirants or deodorants to breast cancer, and a 2014 review of 469 studies found little evidence that aluminium salts increase Alzheimer's risk; it also lists regulatory views on aluminium in antiperspirants [1].

On T Nation, users discussing underarm chafing and stains have mentioned trying different deodorants; one reports switching to a solid stick containing baking soda after skin rashes and yellow stains with another product [5][6]. Another thread asks about persistent body odour that returns after showering [7]. These accounts are individual experiences.

The main listed hazard of sodium bicarbonate on its reference page is serious eye irritation, and the page does not discuss skin irritation [2]. Wikipedia notes that alkaline soaps can disrupt the skin's slightly acidic acid mantle [1]. Some users on social media report underarm rashes from baking soda deodorants; no published study of this was located. The T Nation account above mentions rashes with a different deodorant and none with baking soda [6].

lore.intro: Baking soda deodorant appears in forum discussions about avoiding yellow stains and skin reactions from commercial products.

claims.claim: Baking soda deodorant controls odour without the stains or rashes of commercial deodorants.
Baking soda neutralises the acids that cause odour.

timeline.event: Valentin Rose the Younger credited with discovering sodium bicarbonate in Berlin [2].
Edna Murphey patents Mum, described as the first modern commercial deodorant [1].
US patent for a deodorant pad system using a baking soda solution [3].
